title: Naming Animals
objective: After this level you can explain scientific names and Linnaeus's system.
summary: Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus then species; animal names start from 1758. Species sit inside ranks from domain down, and close relatives share a genus.

cards.headline: Say 'robin' in London and in Boston, and you mean two different birds.
cards.body: Early colonists in America named their bird robin because its breast color reminded them of the smaller European robin. The American robin is about 25 cm long, the European one about 14 cm. Same word, different animals. Scientists needed a better system.

cards.headline: Two words, one animal
cards.body: In the 1700s, Carl Linnaeus replaced long descriptive phrases with a two-part name for each species: first the genus, then the species. The European robin is Erithacus rubecula; the American robin is Turdus migratorius. Biologists everywhere accept the system, so a scientific name points to one species, wherever you are. Yours is Homo sapiens, and Linnaeus picked it himself.

cards.context: That's the year of the 10th edition of Linnaeus's Systema Naturae, the starting point for naming animals. Plants got their starting line a little earlier, with his Species Plantarum in 1753. Think of 1758 as day one of the official animal register.

mascot.line: A whole kingdom, and it all starts with one very long book.

cards.headline: Boxes inside boxes
cards.body: Linnaeus also stacked species into ranks: kingdom, class, order, genus, species. Biologists later added more, and today's ladder runs domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Close relatives share the lower rungs. Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars all sit in the genus Panthera, so the tiger is Panthera tigris and the leopard Panthera pardus. The genus works like a surname.

cards.headline: Names: decoded
learned: Common names can mean different animals in different places
Ranks from domain down to species; relatives share a genus

questions.prompt: In a two-part scientific name like Turdus migratorius, what does the first word name?

options.label: The person who found it
options.rationale: Names honor people sometimes, but the first word is the genus.

options.label: The class
options.rationale: Class is a much bigger rank than the first word.

questions.explanation: A scientific name gives the genus first, then the species.

questions.prompt: Why is 'Erithacus rubecula' more useful than 'robin' when scientists in different countries compare notes?

options.label: It describes the bird's size
options.rationale: The name doesn't give a size.

options.label: It points to one species everywhere
It lists where the bird lives
options.rationale: Scientific names are not range maps.

questions.explanation: 'Robin' means different birds in Europe and America, but a scientific name refers to one species wherever it's used.

questions.prompt: Level 2's species estimate leaned on the bigger groups that species sit inside. Which list gives three of those ranks, from biggest to smallest?

options.label: Genus, family, order
options.rationale: That runs from smallest to biggest.

options.label: Species, genus, kingdom
options.rationale: Species is the smallest rank, not a bigger group.

questions.explanation: Today's ladder runs domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; Mora's team used the better-known higher ranks.
